newsitem.title: UK: What UK's Labour needs to do to join EMU by 2002.
newsitem.headline: What UK's Labour needs to do to join EMU by 2002.

text.p: The ruling UK Labour Party's overtly pro-European stance since last week's landslide election win has raised speculation about Britain warming to a single European currency within the life of this parliament, analysts said.

Within a week of taking power, Labour has agreed to sign the Social Chapter of the Maastricht Treaty, it has given the Bank of England policy independence in line with Treaty guidelines and is thawing UK relations with the rest of the European Union.
Moreover, a news agency report late Wednesday cited a Labour Party source saying sterling could return to the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) at a much lower rate than it is at present.
Although the Treasury has denied the ERM report, the contrast in attitude with the predominantly Euro-sceptic Conservative government has excited financial markets.
While spurred by a retreating dollar, the pound has dropped nearly seven pfennigs against the German mark since talk of the ERM and EMU has resurfaced.
If Labour were to pursue its more pro-European stance to the extent of participating in EMU by 2002 then there is a list of key issues it needs to consider.

* The biggest hurdle to clear before UK membership of EMU is the commitment of both the ruling Labour Party and opposition Conservatives to hold a referendum on the issue if the parliament of the day, in a free vote, decides to join.

* Opinion polls are not encouraging. The last specific poll conducted, a Gallup poll in January, showed only 25 percent of Britons would support a single currency compared with 60 percent in France and more than 70 percent in Italy. However a Reuters/NOP poll last week said Europe was low on the list of voters' priorities with 53 percent saying it would not affect the way they voted in last Thursday's election.

* According to the Maastricht Treaty the UK must exercise its negotiated EMU option before January 1 1998 if it is to take part at the planned start date on January 1, 1999. If it does not do so by year-end, the issue of the UK's involvement is put on ice until the single currency starts.

* The text of the UK EMU option says the UK must act, or "opt-in", if it wants to be involved. Otherwise it will be automatically excluded. The UK can choose to opt-in at any stage once EMU starts in 1999 and such a move would likely coincide with one of the EU's bi-annual reviews of convergence criteria.
* The Maastricht Treaty requires the UK to be a member of the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) for two years without devaluation before entering monetary union.
* If the letter of the Treaty is to be applied, then it is already too late for the UK to take part in the first wave of EMU on January 1999.

* If the UK were to re-join a reconstituted "ERM II" in 1999, which would link non-EMU currencies to the new euro, sterling would satisfy the criterion in time for membership of the the single currency by 2001. This would be before the single currency notes and coins are introduced in 2002 and before the latest date at which the next UK general election can be called.

* Independent forecasts for this year and next show the UK will meet all other economic criteria for joining EMU in 1999. These include targets for outstanding public debt, annual budget deficits, inflation rates and long-term interest rates.

* Not all analysts agree that ERM membership is an absolute necessity, however, because the mechanism was radically altered following the ERM crisis in the summer of 1993. The Maastricht Treaty was written in December 1991. Former UK finance minister Kenneth Clarke said the ERM rule should be defunct as a result.
However, several Bundesbank members and senior EU officials have insisted the ERM criterion remains.
* The UK, Sweden and Greece are the only EU countries currently outside the ERM. The only other country to have a negotiated option on its EMU membership is Denmark.

Many analysts believe the most important net effect of the fresh EMU speculation in the UK will be to keep a lid on the robust pound. Any eventual fixing of the pound in EMU would most likely be at levels lower than the current value around 2.75 marks.

"The government will probably be happy to see sterling's overvaluation unwound and they are probably privately happy to see the effects of this week's speculation," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan.
"We can expect to hear more talk of ERM, EMU and 2.50 targets."
However, many believe Labour will keep its distance from such a domestically divisive subject.
"The Treaty says that if the decision is not taken this year, there's nothing they can do before 1999," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"Unless there appears to be glaring costs to remaining outside the project, the attitude will most likely be 'why bother?'"
